title: Super nervous to post my game at all
author: LeVuS87
selftext:
Spent weeks working on it, and I know that’s not very long and it’s not perfect and probably shouldn’t be launching it but I feel like getting something out there and learning from the process is going to help me be better for next time.

Started out with a completely different prototype, built with Sol 5.6 and in Godot, similar premise just kiting around a creature for X amount of time.

It was fine, but not quite the experience I was wanting.

Then I revamped it using Astra, built out the game loop a feature at a time, created a new creature using Meshy and Blender MCP, had Astra build out the whole motel fairly quickly with Blender MCP and in Unreal.

It was fine, and I published the coming soon page for Steam. As soon as it got approved I had regrets. My creature felt like a generic slop witch and the animations needed improvement for sure.

So I decided to redesign it. Using Meshy again, GPT-Image-2.5, Astra and Opus 5.5 I iterated through each model and the creature until it felt a little more polished. Sound effects with Eleven Labs, music with Google Flow Music. None of this was one shotted, not a single item, my workflow was mostly:

AI generates a small slice -> I test it/look at it/listen to it -> I berate AI to feel better about myself and tell it what to do differently -> Repeat until happy

And I think the end result is fun and something that I’m happy with but it’s hard to tell because I get tunnel vision and maybe it’s not good, but at the end of the day I overall enjoyed making it, and I hope some people enjoy playing it. 

Wouldn’t mind for as many people as possible to add to wishlist.

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5300960/KEEP\_IT\_ON\_HER/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5300960/KEEP_IT_ON_HER/)

Also Opus 5.5 made both of my trailers, recording the gameplay footage after we went a few rounds on direction and me telling it the footage is bad.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Creepy looking monster. Liked the way she peeked around the door frame. 

One thing that bothered me a bit while watching was how static the flashlight/hand is while it's such an important part of your game. Consider taking a look at how Resident Evil handles there's, where you get a lot more motion from the flashlight (or when they have like a lighter or something they're using for light.) You get a real feel for the emotions of the character too, depending on how they're holding it. Might really help with the immersion in this. 

Good luck!

comments.author: m-freak
comments.body:
Mm, the graphics are fine, but the writing clearly has that AI nonsense going on. You should at least edit it? None of it properly gives off horror vibes, and when people see confusing writing that's clearly AI with no human refinement put into it, they're gonna turn away. A good chunk of people are fine with AI, but are mostly just worried about slop - and slop shows in the writing first, which is the fastest way to get people who aren't willing to just try anything AI out (unless the game will be free? you kind of have to convince people to part with money, though, and many others won't even be good about parting with time they'll never get back and could spend playing games they're more sure they might like and that has effort in it).

"Look away and she's already smiling". Besides being a bit of a clear AI trying to imitate creepy things but not having feelings, what does this contribute? She's kind of always smiling anyway? Without the animation to back this up, it's useless. It's a cheap shot that doesn't trigger anything because there's no other emotion to flicker between.

The AI also isn't giving any sense of urgency or writing like you'd expect for a horror game, either. Genre expectations exist for a reason and horror fans are usually just as fickle and precise as romance fans - they know what they like and they expect any subversion of expectations to actually pay out. But this isn't a subversion of expectations, it's just an AI TELLING what's supposed to make the game creepy rather than showing.

"Do the job" is where it already starts rocky. "The job" is vague and with the boring, bland sentence, it already feels like something nobody cares about. What is the job? When people play games where you balance horror and tasks, they want to know what they're doing. So what are we doing? Cleaning? Even if you want to be more vague, you could inject more urgency in it. "Try to complete the tasks while she hunts you down" alone would be a good direction.

And the rest of the trailer captions are, what I said, a whole bunch of yapping about the basic game mechanics that you could find in any mascot horror game that doesn't give a lick of flavor about why people should spend their time on YOUR mascot horror game. "Doors slow her down. They don't stop her. She's never where you left her. One touch and you're done." I could replace this with literally any weeping angel style mascot horror. Horror games in this genre usually also care about lore. Besides the lack of urgency, there's a lack of anything interesting about her besides her design. What is the lore??? Where's the hints of mystery and crumbs of why people should be invested in this game?

Art direction and design is like, one piece. Video games are a marriage of the arts. You still need things like narrative direction. 

"You're the night clerk, the front door is locked, and the guests still want towels. Sweetie wants you. She only freezes while your flashlight is on her. Look away and she's already smiling. One touch and you're checked out. Permanently." All of this has the same issue the trailer captions do. What's interesting about it? It's a bunch of basic mascot horror mechanics and tropes thrown together. It's the game dev version of going onto booktop and slopping together the words "alpha male + mafia + enemies to lovers" while people don't know a single damn thing about the actual characters or worldbuilding. It also needs an injection of urgency and lore put in it.

It doesn't matter how good your game is; they'll flop if the marketing is ass, and copywriting is part of marketing. 

The actual page does better with telling you what you're doing, and it gives a bit of "she's crazy". But like, why? Why would someone be interested in her instead of just replaying Bendy and the Ink Machine? What keeps player retention? What makes them care about your game, world, or character? Mascot horror DOES need characterization work. All of the endless repetition of the same features over and over could be replaced and filled with more meaningful content to actually get players hooked. You need to be genre-aware when doing anything creative, and genuinely think about what the audience is usually interested in and looking for.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
Agreed. AI slop most often means graphically and visual presentation but it doesn’t have to be. Slop can be a half baked idea, half baked execution, incomplete concept. It mainly is just a game that isn’t as polished and complete as it should be.

In this case it just feels more like a mini game than a game. The trailer basically is just telling me my sole focus of the game is to… not die and keep the flashlight on her. Which in itself is a little confusing because if I keep my flashlight on her I assume I am just staring at her the entire time and by direct consequence NOT getting away. So what is the objective exactly?

To make a good game in a genre one has to truly study the greats in that genre. What are some of the best examples in the horror genre? What makes them great? Anticipation right?

Where is the anticipation if I see the monster 50 times in the trailer? Did M night shamalayan get famous by showing monsters 50 times in the trailer of his movies? 

I think the game has decent visual polish to the point where I wouldn’t call it visual slop. But as a horror film fan, there’s nothing about this that makes me want to play it; free or paid, to be honest.

replies.author: m-freak
replies.body:
Yes! There's clearly art design and an idea in mind! It's not just a general "abandoned building with creaky, rusty textures" and "obscurely scary monster". But art direction alone and no other follow-through is how you get a massive disappointment like Subliminal, where it looks great but you can kind of tell when the devs kind of just didn't know wtf they were doing besides making nice backgrounds or thinking of playstyle and the gamer experience.

The average gamer may not be thinking of how important narrative design and lore and characterization is - but there's a small, yet important thing you're taught about both game dev and 3D modeling. 

And that's the rule of: "Viewers won't notice it's there, but they'll CERTAINLY notice it's NOT there."

So as a dev/artist, you don't have the luxury of not thinking about what the gamers/viewers don't! You have to go deeper.

comments.author: deReaLizedGames
comments.body:
I think it looks fantastic! The graphics, enemy animation, and lighting are really good.

I agree about the hand movement. If you give it some sway on both walking and camera movement/sway it'll go a long way. I'd add camera sway with mouse movement + head bobbing for walking too - those are classic horror game staples. If you do both of these, it'll give the game more "juice," and make it feel more immersive/add to the horror ambiance. And they should both be pretty easy to implement with AI too.
